# 3 Maccabees Chapter 4 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Greek MS (Codex Alexandrinus) | **Section:** The Jews Imprisoned in the Hippodrome

---

**1** Wherever this decree arrived, a festival was proclaimed among the Gentiles, with joy and gladness, the hatred that had been hidden for so long now breaking out openly.

**2** But among the Jews there was incessant mourning, lamentation, and tearful crying; their hearts were on fire with grief as they mourned over what had happened to them so suddenly.

**3** What district or city, what inhabited place or what streets, were not filled with weeping and lamentation over them?

**4** They were driven out under such bitter and pitiless compulsion by the generals in the various cities that at the sight of their extraordinary sufferings even some of their enemies were moved to pity and reflected on the uncertainty of life, thinking that these same reversals might befall them too at any time.

**5** A host of old men with white hair, bent over from the harsh treatment they had suffered along the way, their legs bowed from old age and shame, were driven along.

**6** Young women who had just entered the marriage chamber to share in the joys of wedded life, with their faces veiled in sorrow rather than in joy, and who exchanged their fragrant ointments for unwashed hair, were driven along; and instead of wedding songs they were escorted with lamentations.

**7** They were dragged along forcibly in their bonds, in full public view.

**8** In public disgrace and wretched misery they were thrust aboard ships and brought with their children to Alexandria.

**9** When they arrived there, the king gave orders that they be concentrated in the hippodrome that stood before the city.

**10** The place was enormous and magnificently suited to such a scene; it was in a position to expose them to the view of all who entered or left the city and of all who went in to the royal palace.

**11** This was done out of pure malice, so that those who had been stripped of all their possessions would also be put to public shame.

**12** And there, imprisoned as though they were condemned criminals awaiting death, the Jews waited.

**13** Now there was one Hermon, the elephant keeper, and Ptolemy had ordered him to take his five hundred war elephants, get them drunk on unmixed wine mixed with frankincense, and then release them against the Jews in the early morning, so that they would be trampled underfoot.

**14** In this way all the Jews who were packed together in the hippodrome would be destroyed.

**15** But when the king had given these orders, the friends who were present, seeing his extreme and groundless cruelty toward the Jews, pleaded with him to cancel the order, saying:

**16** O king, do not act in this way! Do not bring ruin upon your kingdom by dealing so cruelly with those who have done no wrong.

**17** But the king was filled with rage and paid no attention to their words.

**18** When morning came, however, the order had not been carried out, and the guards reported to the king that the elephants had not been made ready.

**19** The king was greatly angered and threatened Hermon and his men with punishment for this failure.

**20** But Hermon and his officers excused themselves, saying that the elephants had not been given the wine in time.

**21** The king therefore postponed the punishment to the following day and issued the order again.

**22** All that day the assembled Jews in the hippodrome prayed to God with tears and lamentation.

**23** They called upon the Almighty Lord, the Master of all power, their merciful God and Father, imploring him to turn aside the evil plot that was being carried out against them.
